title: Mitigating synchronization bottlenecks in high-performance actor-model-based software
problem: Bulk synchronous programming and fork-join patterns require frequent synchronization which severely undermines performance in parallel systems. Scaling the actor model to handle hundreds of thousands of short-lived tasks efficiently requires mitigating these synchronization bottlenecks.
motivation: Synchronization overhead is a critical performance limiter in distributed and shared-memory parallel systems, and optimizing the actor model for HPC could provide a more flexible alternative to MPI.
method: The approach uses the actor model (a way to write parallel programs where independent computing units called actors send messages to each other) to handle hundreds of thousands of short-lived tasks efficiently. Instead of processing each message individually—which forces the system to pause and synchronize frequently—messages are batched together (grouped and processed in bulk). This batching reduces synchronization overhead (the expensive cost of coordinating between tasks), allowing the system to flexibly handle both uniform and varied computing tasks.
key_novelty: Batching actor messages together (processing them in groups rather than one at a time) reduces the overhead of coordinating between tasks, making the actor model competitive or superior to MPI and OpenMP on large-scale parallel computing problems.
contributions: Actor batching technique for buffering communication to reduce synchronization bottlenecks
Load balancing strategy for hundreds of thousands of short-lived tasks in actor-based systems
Demonstration of 4x speedup with buffering versus unbuffered actor model
Competitive performance against MPI and OpenMP on continental-scale hydrologic simulations

metrics.speedup: ~4x with buffering versus unbuffered; outperforms MPI on single/multiple nodes; competitive with OpenMP (single node) and MPI+OpenMP (multiple nodes)

limitations: Evaluation limited to single hydrologic simulation application (500K+ element continental domain); generalization and scalability to other HPC domains not discussed.
